data.description: Welcome to Pharmaceutical Executive Daily, your quick briefing on the top news shaping the pharmaceutical and life sciences industry.

data.title: <![CDATA[FDA Shelves Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher Program: Report ]]>
data.description:
FDA shelved the fast-track drug review initiative during the Trump administration by former Commissioner , according to six sources familiar with the matter and internal documents.1

The Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher (CNPV) program was launched in June 2025, and was designed to slash drug review timelines to just one to two months for therapies addressing national priorities, such as urgent unmet health needs. The program was met with controversy however, as concerns rose over possible preferential treatment for companies meeting demands of President Donald Trump, such as offering drugs at lower prices.

Holly Fernandez Lynch, a health policy professor at the University of Pennsylvania, describes the program as “the worst of both worlds,” combining serious risks of political influence with potentially limited practical benefit, since many drugs might have qualified for other speedy review pathways.1

The program was once touted as a bold fix for U.S. pharmaceutical regulation, but the program has instead been left adrift, mostly due to a lack of steady at FDA, which has been without a permanent commissioner since May.1 As of today, 22 total drugs have been given a voucher, while a dozen have been approved, including five since Makary left FDA in May.2 Since Makary’s departure, no new drugs have received a voucher.1

data.title: <![CDATA[Eli Lilly Breaks Ground on $3.5 billion Pennsylvania Manufacturing Site]]>
data.description:
Eli Lilly and Company broke ground on a $3.5 billion manufacturing facility in Pennsylvania’s Lehigh Valley.

The site joins nine other new U.S. manufacturing sites Eli Lilly has announced since 2020, and is one of four among them dedicated to injectable medicines and devices. The project is part of the company’s $50 billion push to expand medicine production in the U.S., and the Lehigh Valley site is expected to add capacity for the next generation of obesity treatments, including retatrutide, a first-in-class investigational GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon triple hormone receptor agonist.1

David A. Ricks, chair and chief executive officer, Lilly, ties the investment directly to the pace of innovation in obesity care. “Obesity is one of the biggest health challenges of our time, and the science to treat it is moving quickly,” says Ricks. “Retatrutide is one of several next-generation medicines we’re developing that could help millions more people living with obesity, type 2 diabetes, or both. This $3.5 billion investment means we’ll be able to make these medicines in Pennsylvania for people here at home and around the world.”

What will the Lehigh Valley site produce, and when will it open?

The Lehigh Valley site, located in Fogelsville, Pennsylvania, was originally earlier in the year in February, and is expected to be operational by 2031. The site will add manufacturing capacity for next-generation obesity treatments, including retatrutide, which Lilly is studying in several Phase III clinical trials evaluating its potential efficacy and safety in obesity and overweight with at least one weight-related medical problem, type 2 diabetes, knee osteoarthritis pain, moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea, chronic low back pain, cardiovascular outcomes, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.2

data.title: <![CDATA[Moderna Lays Out Oncology-Driven Growth Plan at 2026 Analyst Day]]>
data.description:
Moderna, Inc outlined it’s next phase of growth strategy at 2026 Analyst Day, highlighting how more than a decade of investment in the company’s mRNA platform has enabled the development of multiple modalities of mRNA medicines, each with the potential to create durable franchises.

The company also provided updates on commercial growth, oncology pipeline progress, manufacturing readiness, and mid-term financial objectives.

What is Moderna’s business strategy?

Moderna’s strategy rests on an integrated mRNA platform that combines mRNA science, delivery technologies, and manufacturing capabilities.1 By developing modalities that share underlying technologies and processes, the company is aiming to improve development efficiency and capital productivity while expanding the range of potential applications for mRNA medicines.1 Moderna has developed three established modalities spanning infectious disease vaccines, individualized cancer treatments, and rare genetic liver diseases, with intismeran advancing toward potential commercialization following positive Phase III results in adjuvant melanoma, subject to regulatory approval.2

The company is identifying commercial growth opportunities for 2027 and beyond including seasonal influenza, where Moderna is preparing for a broader commercial launch during the 2027-2028 respiratory season.1 In Europe, the company now has four approved respiratory vaccines in the European Union and is positioned for additional growth as a competitor’s Covid-19 vaccine contract expires. Long-term strategic partnerships in the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia provide recurring revenue and support domestic manufacturing, while new agreements in Mexico and Taiwan are set to expand opportunities in Latin America and Asia-Pacific.1

data.title: <![CDATA[Pfizer and Blackstone Sign Co-Funding Deal for berobenatide]]>
data.description:
Pfizer Inc. and Blackstone Life Sciences entered a strategic co-funding agreement under which funds managed by Blackstone will pay upwards of $1.5 billion in development costs through 2028 for berobenatide.

The investigational, potential first-in-class monthly GLP-1 receptor agonist peptide is currently being studied for chronic weight management and obesity-related conditions. In exchange for the funding, Blackstone will be eligible to receive milestone-based payments, subject to U.S. regulatory approval of monthly dosing of injectable berobenatide monotherapy for chronic weight management and the achievement of certain commercial sales milestones.1

Cecile Guegan, chief financial officer and executive vice president, Pfizer, frames the agreement as part of a broader financing strategy for the company’s pipeline. “Our aim is to bring important new medicines to patients while taking a disciplined approach that pairs internal research investments with targeted investment from capital partners,” Guegan says. “Today’s announcement helps us advance our comprehensive obesity program and maintain the financial capacity and flexibility to invest in our broader pipeline across all therapeutic areas.”

What are the terms of the agreement?

Blackstone-managed funds are set to cover up to $1.5 billion of berobenatide’s development costs through 2028.1 In return, Blackstone becomes eligible for milestone-based payments tied to two conditions: U.S. regulatory approval of monthly dosing of injectable berobenatide monotherapy for chronic weight management, and the achievement of certain commercial sales milestones once the product reaches the market.1 The structure is expected to keep Blackstone purely as a capital partner rather than a stakeholder in the asset itself, as it holds no rights or ownership in berobenatide, while Pfizer continues to run the program’s operations and make its development decisions.1

data.title: <![CDATA[FDA Approves Pimjetmi for Patients With Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor]]>
data.description:
Merck KGaA received FDA approval for Pimjetmi (pimicotinib), a once-daily oral colony stimulating factor-1 receptor (CSF-1R) inhibitor, as a systemic treatment for adults with symptomatic tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT) for whom surgical resection may cause worsening functional limitation or severe morbidity.

The approval gives patients who are not good candidates for surgery a new oral option for a disease that has historically been managed primarily through operative intervention.

Danny Bar-Zohar, chief executive officer healthcare and member of the executive board of Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, frames the approval as both a patient-focused and strategic milestone. “People living with TGCT have long faced difficult treatment decisions as they navigate a disease that can significantly affect their daily lives including their mobility,” Bar-Zohar says. “Translating scientific innovation into clinically meaningful advances for people living with rare tumors is a strategic imperative for our company, as we continue our commitment to addressing significant unmet needs. With the approval of Pimjetmi in the U.S., we strengthen our leadership position and growing portfolio in rare tumors and bring real hope to patients and their families.”
